---
title: "Workflow graphs"
description: "Draws an overview of a repository's GitHub Actions workflows into .github/workflow-graphs/README.md."
---

`workflow-graphs.yml` writes an overview of your repository's GitHub
Actions workflows — a table and diagrams — and keeps it up to date in
`.github/workflow-graphs/README.md`. GitHub shows that file when someone
opens the `.github/workflow-graphs/` folder, next to `.github/workflows/` —
close to where people look to understand how the repository's automation
works, without cluttering the README for your package's users.

It is generated from the workflow files alone, with no AI involved: the
same files always give the same overview.

## What you get

A high-level overview of what exists — for the details of a workflow,
its file is the place to look.

- **A table** of all workflows — name, file, what starts them, which
  reusable workflows they call (with owner, repository, file and
  version), and what they produce, with the condition where there is one
  ("Issue for the PR author — *if check fails*"). Several entries in a
  cell are listed as bullets.
- **Events**: one small diagram per event — a pull request into `dev`, a
  pull request into `main`, a closed pull request, a schedule, a push —
  with the workflows it starts, what they produce, and the workflows they
  start in turn (dotted arrows). What a workflow produces follows the
  order of its jobs: for a release, the check comes first, then "PR
  merged" if it succeeds or an issue if it fails, and the merge starts the
  publishing. Conditions are written in words — **only if:** (it happens
  only then, e.g. when certain files changed) and **skipped:** (it
  doesn't happen then) — once in a workflow's box when they apply to
  everything it does, on the arrow when they differ. A workflow with
  several triggers appears under each event, showing what it produces
  there.

GitHub draws the diagrams itself ([Mermaid](https://mermaid.js.org)), so
the README is plain text: changes show up as readable diffs. How the
overview is put together — your own text around it, where "what a workflow
produces" comes from, and what it can't show — is on
[How the overview is built](workflow-graphs-details.qmd).

## When it runs

| Event | What happens |
|---|---|
| Push to the branch where merges land (e.g. `dev`) | The README is updated and committed directly: `docs: update workflow diagrams`. A `docs:` commit never triggers a release. |
| Pull request | Nothing is committed — a commit can't be placed on a pull request. One short comment says so, pointing to the trigger to use instead. Don't trigger it on pull requests. |
| Manual run | Like a push, on the branch you pick. |

The example below runs on changes to `.github/workflows/` only. The README
lives outside that folder, so updating it doesn't start another run.

::: {.callout-note}
## Protected branch
If the branch requires pull requests, the direct commit needs to bypass
that rule: add the [GitHub App](getting-started.qmd#github-app) as a bypass
actor for that branch, as for `main` in the
[release](branch-protection.qmd).
:::
